newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military shows off 21st century war tactics.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military shows off 21st century war tactics.

text.p: A soldier clicks his laptop mouse five times and presses enter, and somewhere over the horizon an enemy tank explodes 30 seconds later.
Whoosh, and welcome to digital warfare, real video games played this month in the most sophisticated ground war tests yet by the U.S. military of its plans for the next century.

Using more than $250 million in sophisticated new electronics against an "enemy" army in a mock desert battle, a specially equipped 7,000-member Experimental Force based at Ft. Hood, Texas moved onto this Mojavie Desert base this week to repel a similar-sized "Red Force" invading mythical U.S. ally, Mojavia.

Defence Secretary William Cohen flew in on Tuesday to look at the technology that will drive wars in the next century. After a day of roaming the dust-blown desert battlefield by helicopter and Humvee ground vehicle, he left impressed.
"Today, I have seen the future of warfare," he told reporters travelling with him. "What you are seeing here is a revolution of warfare ... this is the future and there is no turning back."

A tank sergeant showed Cohen how, with five simple clicks of a computer mouse, he could direct F-16 jet and artillery strikes on an enemy tank on the other side of a craggy sand ridge. It took less than 30 seconds for a computer-game-like picture to pop up on his laptop screen, photographed and videotaped by an unmanned drone 11,000 feet (3,000 metres) above the desert floor, out of range of enemy missiles, showing the "kill."
Sgt. George Thomison, from Kaw City, Oklahoma, jokes as he deftly handles his computer mouse that "I never could handle Pac-Man," one of the earliest and least complex computer games.

The Army tests will be conducted over the next few weeks using high-flying drones, satellites, J-Star planes like those used over Bosnia to identify every vehicle within 250 miles (400 km) and other space age wizardry.

The aim is to give men on the ground real-time photographs and video images beamed down day and night. The detailed information would keep armoured columns moving through dust storms, guided from above. Alarms would sound when approaching mine fields, and there would be fewer "friendly fire" deaths.

Critics argue that the equipment is too fragile, expensive and difficult to use for a full-fledged digital army. They say that in the heat of a real battle too much incoming information would thicken the fog, not clear it away.
The non-partisan General Accounting Office watchdog agency estimates it would cost a minimum of $4 billion to equip all 10 Army divisions with gear similar to what is being used here.
In the first few days of the mock battle across mountain passes and over rocky desolate valleys of this Rhode Island-sized base, there were some notable breakdowns.

An infantry unit marched right through a narrow gap in a ridge into a waiting enemy-held position and were "slimed," as the Army put it, because the wrong map grid coordinates were sent by controllers.
And four out of seven Apache helicopters were "zapped" by the enemy when they tried to penetrate too deep behind enemy lines based on a faulty reading during a post-midnight raid.
Army officers said some glitches are to be expected and they were generally pleased with the testing.

Col. Marshall Townsend, a deputy director of the National Training Centre based here who is monitoring the battle from a tented Tactical Operation Centre in the desert, said that so far the most impressive performance came from the drones. In the air eight to 10 hours at a time, using infrared and other cameras, the Unmanned Air Vehicles buzz over any selected target.
"They provide terrific real-time snapshots of the action that we use to direct fire," he said of the slow-flying planes controlled like high-tech model planes from a dry lake bed base.

Maj. Gen. Paul Kern, head of the Experimental Force, said his troops' technological advantages helped scored some initial successes in deep-behind-the-lines attacks. They were able to find targets in the dead of night and destroy them.

But by midday on Tuesday, the enemy "Red Force," a veteran unit based here that fights mock battles year-round using Soviet-style MiGs and weapons, had halted advance units using chemical weapons and other traditional tactics.
